name: Facial symmetry theory

lead: Facial symmetry theory holds that faces with closely matching left and right sides look more attractive and healthier. Looksmaxxers use it as a guide for what to even out first, through grooming, hairstyle and posture, and in some cases fillers or surgery.

Research since the 1990s, including Grammer and Thornhill (1994), reports that symmetrical faces tend to get higher attractiveness ratings, independently of averageness. Later work found the effect for both sexes, stronger for female faces. The picture is mixed: effects differ by rating method, and some researchers argue symmetry matters mainly because it makes a face look typical. Links to objective health are described as inconsistent.

paras: People check symmetry in front-facing photos or mirror-flipped images, then work on what they can: hair parting, brow shaping, beard shaping, sleeping and chewing habits, posture. Forum guides also discuss fillers, implants and bone-related methods, and the effect of posture or non-surgical methods is untested.

The theory carries no direct risk. Clinical literature notes that marked asymmetry from conditions such as facial palsy or craniofacial microsomia affects quality of life and is treated medically or surgically. Community guides on correcting symmetry include procedures with their own medical risks.

angle.text: Looksmaxxers use symmetry as a guide for what to even out first, so the face reads as more balanced and healthy, trying grooming, fillers, implants or posture work. Studies find a real but modest link between symmetry and attractiveness.

lead: Facial symmetry theory is the proposal that bilateral symmetry of the face makes it more attractive and that this preference reflects an evolved sensitivity to cues of health and developmental stability. Researchers distinguish fluctuating asymmetry, random left-right differences, from directional asymmetry, a consistent bias across a population. [1]

A widely cited study by Grammer and Thornhill (1994) used computer-generated faces and reported that men and women preferred averageness and symmetry in opposite-sex faces. [2] Later work found that symmetry increases attractiveness ratings for both sexes, with stronger effects reported for female faces, and that symmetry and averageness contribute independently. [1]

Evidence for the health side of the theory is more mixed. Studies report that more symmetrical faces are rated as healthier, but links to objective health measures are described as inconsistent, and some researchers argue symmetry matters mainly through making a face look normal. [1][3][4] On looksmax.org symmetry is a staple topic, with guides on improving it and threads arguing about its importance.

paras: Facial symmetry is one component, alongside averageness and youthfulness, that shapes judgments of physical attractiveness. Directional asymmetry is common: a well-known example is a slight leftward offset of eyes, nose and mouth relative to the ears, about 2 degrees at birth and about 0.5 degrees in adults. [1]

A clinical review notes that perfect facial symmetry has long been considered a hallmark of beauty but is almost elusive in nature, while clinically evident skeletal asymmetry is common and can arise from congenital deformities, developmental abnormalities or trauma.  A plastic surgery review lists symmetry among the classic tenets of beauty, with phi, averageness, youthfulness and sexual dimorphism.

Grammer and Thornhill (1994), working from parasite theory of sexual selection, had participants rate computer images of faces and composites and reported preferences for symmetry and averageness. [2] Kowner (1996) used mirrored face halves, and Rhodes and colleagues (1998) found symmetry mattered more for female faces. [1]

Perrett and colleagues (1999) found that symmetrical transformation made older faces more attractive but could make young adult and child faces less attractive, and noted that mirroring can create artifacts such as an oversized nose half. [1]

subs.h: Studies of men's and women's faces
paras: A 1999 study of men's faces with measured symmetry examined whether women use symmetry as a primary cue of phenotypic quality or whether it correlates with other facial markers affecting attractiveness. [3] A 2001 study examined symmetry and sexual dimorphism in male facial proportions, and a 2004 study looked at symmetry, averageness and feature size in the facial attractiveness of women. [5][6] A 1999 study also examined human body odour, symmetry and attractiveness. [7]

A study discussed on looksmax.org proposed that symmetry increases attractiveness only when it also makes a face look more normal or typical, and reported that altering Chinese male faces sometimes reduced attractiveness because the symmetrical version looked less natural. This explanation is offered for why past studies disagreed.  Grokipedia likewise reports that the symmetry-attractiveness association may be mediated by averageness or normality and shrinks when perceived health is controlled. [4]

Scheib, Gangestad and Thornhill (1999) examined symmetry as a cue of good genes, and Jones and colleagues (2001, 2004) found symmetrical faces were rated as healthier with better perceived skin condition. [1][3] Klingenberg and colleagues (2010) suggested asymmetry may reflect prenatal stress exposures such as alcohol rather than inferior genes. [1]

Grokipedia reports that links between symmetry and objective health measures, such as immune function, are inconsistent, that fluctuating asymmetry is not a stand-alone diagnostic tool, and that dynamic symmetry, such as an uneven smile, may matter more than resting symmetry. [4]

Wikipedia also summarizes mixed findings on personality, including positive links between facial symmetry and extraversion, while noting that judging character from faces is widely regarded as pseudoscience though it continues to be studied. [1]

Clinical literature on facial asymmetry focuses on restoration rather than attractiveness. Reviews cover craniofacial microsomia, Parry-Romberg syndrome (progressive hemifacial atrophy), skeletal asymmetry treated with orthognathic surgery, and facial palsy managed with botulinum toxin and exercise.  A systematic review of botulinum toxin for facial palsy states that facial asymmetry correlates strongly with impaired social interaction and self-image.

Studies of symmetry and attractiveness are perception experiments, not clinical trials; examples include the 1994, 1999, 2001 and 2004 studies above. [2][3][5][6] Randomized trials exist for facial symmetry in patients with Bell's palsy: a 2024 trial in India compared a facial stretching program with structured exercise against conventional exercise, and a 2022 trial tested a 'Mirror Effect Plus Protocol' in acute severe Bell's palsy.  No clinical trials were found testing whether altering facial symmetry in healthy people changes attractiveness or social outcomes.

Looksmax.org threads range from a claim that facial symmetry is the only indicator of attractiveness, to a long guide in which the author argues that symmetrical faces are naturally beautiful and recommends addressing symmetry before implants or fillers.  Other threads discuss the sphenoid bone, the eye area and the effect of posture on symmetry.
Some members cite research indicating that symmetry's effects are inconsistent.

lore.intro: Symmetry is among the most discussed facial traits on the forum, with members both prioritizing it and disputing its importance.

claims.claim: Facial symmetry is the main driver of attractiveness.
Fix symmetry first, before implants or fillers.
